newsitem.title: UK: Metaleurop sees zinc market improving.
newsitem.headline: Metaleurop sees zinc market improving.

text.p: Zinc prices should rise and lead prices remain stable at high levels in the medium term, said Helmut Stodieck, chairman of metal group Metaleurop SA.

At a presentation to the Association of Mining Analysts on Tuesday he said the company would continue to focus on its core lead and zinc markets while developing niche special metal operations and its downstream businesses.
"We will stay a lead and zinc producer," Stodieck said.
"Metaleurop believes in the future of these markets and we will ensure we stay competitive in the not easy conditions in Europe," he added.
Metaleurop is the world's second largest lead producer with annual output of 360,000 tonnes. It is also the seventh largest producer of zinc with annual output of 245,000 tonnes.
He said lead demand rose 22 percent between 1985 and 1995, driven by growth in its largest end-use, the battery industry.
Zinc consumption rose 32 percent over the same period, boosted by the growth of its biggest single user, the galvanizing industry.
Stodieck said he expected demand for both to continue on a similar growth path. Any major progress in electric car battery technology would boost the rate of lead demand growth, he said.
For lead, he said prices were likely to remain at around current high levels during the peak demand period of winter and spring, after which they would probably ease.
The outlook for zinc prices was more bullish now the huge overhang of stocks which built up in the early 1990s had been largely worked off.
"In my view we are close to an area where the decline in stocks should have a marked effect (on prices)," Stodieck said.
"In the region of 450,000 to 500,000 tonnes we should feel a price effect from this development," he added.
London Metal Exchange (LME) inventories now stand at 549,050 tonnes, down from the peak of over 1.2 million tonnes in late 1994.
Stodieck said Metaleurop would continue to operate chiefly in Europe, where its main customer base was situated.
"We are always looking for opportunities, but I don't see us buying into a smelter in the near future (outside Europe)," Stodieck said.
He said problems with the new Nordenham lead plant would hit profits for the year as a whole, but added that the market impact of the unexpected closure in August was limited.
"We were in a position to deliver more or less our commitments," he said.

Stodieck said Metaleurop wanted to continue to increase the percentage of secondary metal it produced, because this would provide higher margins, be good for the environment and decrease price volatility for the group.

Last year's purchase by Swiss group Glencore of 15 percent of the capital of Metaleurop had strengthened Metaleurop's position in regions outside Europe, but their importance remained small relative to Europe.

Stodieck said Glencore's involvement in the group was also beneficial because it had the effect of driving down freight costs involved in shipping metal concentrates from South America to Metaleurop plants in Europe.
Glencore is due to take over operation of the group's indium sales to Japan shortly, while Metaleurop will maintain control of its indium sales to Europe, he said.
Metaleurop is the world's largest indium producer.
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
